speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: COMMEMORATION OF SERVICE MEN AND WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me as Minister of Veterans Affairs to remind all Hon. Members that next Friday is Remembrance Day.
I will have the happy duty next week of accompanying a number of First World War veterans to Vimy Ridge. For these veterans it will have been 65 years since the Armistice ending the First World War signalled their salvation. They had survived the bloodiest conflict in history, and bequeathed to Canada a reputation for gallantry that has been untarnished by time. Remembrance Day was intended to commemorate the memory of those who lost their lives in the "war to end all wars", but on November 11 Canadians will also be honouring the victims of later conflicts.
Next year, Mr. Speaker, another generation of Canadians will be returning to France to recall the fortieth Anniversary of D-Day, the day that returned hope and freedom to millions of Europeans held prisoner in their own lands.
Last month, Canadians went overseas to honour the sacrifice of those killed in yet another war. A delegation went to the Far East to mark the thirtieth Anniversary of the end of the Korean conflict. The welcome given to these Canadians by the people of Korea left no doubt about the enduring respect our forces won in the service of the United Nations. Mr. Speaker, more than 110,000 of our countrymen and women died in those wars. Many others returned home with injuries that would be a permanent reminder of the pain of war.
Next Friday, on the sixty-fifth anniversary of the event that led to Remembrance Day, we should, above all, remind ourselves that Canada's commitment to the almost three-quarter million veterans alive today and their families has no cut-off date, no sunset clause. This commitment continues until the last veteran and the last dependant of a veteran has passed away. They gave of their best, and, in return, they deserve the best.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: COMMEMORATION OF SERVICE MEN AND WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), our critic for Veterans Affairs, for affording me the opportunity in joining with the Minister in this tribute, an opportunity I have never sought in the lengthy time that I have been in this House.
Sixty-six years ago, on November 11, 1918, the guns were stilled on the Western Front and Allied and German troops fraternized in the mud of Flanders. Some 41 years ago, the sons and daughters of these same men once again laid down their arms after years of the most horrendous carnage the world had seen, involving battle-fronts in all the corners of the world. Such was our good fortune historically that the gods of war stayed away from our shores in this country, except for brief incursions in 1759, 1774, and 1812-14.
Today, the fires of war are flaring in the Caribbean and Central America as two conflicting world philosophies meet in deadly confrontation. It is our hope, and that of all men solicitous for the continuation in prosperity and hope of the human race, that diplomacy, understanding, and mutual selfinterest, will outlaw war from this planet.
Today, with hope for the future and reverence for the past, we mark the deeds of those who have passed into the shades of history. Although vanished, they have gained immortality for their achievements.
Men and women fought and died 40 years ago-and many who fought are still living-so that freedom should not perish. Freedom to those of us who are veterans was more than an abstraction, more than an ideal to serve as a centre-piece for commencement addresses. Freedom was something we understood in the very fibre of our natures, something without which life was not worth living.
Freedom is that without which all of the other blessings of human living become merely ashes. Freedom is man's capacity to pursue individual goals as well as the goals set by society. Freedom is the right to create, to preserve, to nourish the original flashes of human genius without requiring the approval of the state. Freedom is man's right to reach for the stars, whether or not his grasp is adequate to attain the creative ideals which his nature conjures up.
The exercise of real freedom demands peace. There can be no full exercise of freedom in war, where everything is subordinated to the military objective. No society can be more desirous of peace, more anxious to attain it, and more eager to preserve it, than a free society.
The upward movement of the human mind required to produce great literature, art, ballet, technology and other creative arts must have that free play of the human mind which comes only with peace. The free world is dedicated to the cause of peace and the freedom of men's minds that goes with it. We shall do all that must be done to preserve it, and shall avoid everything that threatens its attainment.
COMMONS DEBATES_______________________________November 4, 1983
Remembrance Day
While the cause of freedom must never intrude in the domestic affairs of others, nevertheless it must be prepared to respond when freedom is endangered. Freedom cannot be imposed on those who reject it, but it cannot be withheld from those who are willing to make an effort to retain it or to attain it.
Recently, in this House of Commons, Prime Minister Thatcher of Great Britain said, "It is time for freedom to take the offensive." Freedom cannot take the offensive by closing its eyes to the incursions of those who sponsor aggression and total control over minds and bodies. Justice may be blind but freedom cannot be, if it intends to survive. Nor can freedom be the cherished possession of the few while denied to the restless and helpless millions around the world.
Freedom stems from the very nature of humanity, from the fact that men and women are gifted with intelligence and the capacity to choose for themselves. By so much as they are denied that right, by so much does humanity suffer.
When creative thinking is placed at the service of the state and reduced to a servile status so that the best and greatest minds are denied the capacity to function creatively, then this is an assault on the very nature of man.
Joseph Howe, in the early days of this nation, had this to say:
Let a wise nation preserve its monuments, decorate the graves of its illustrious dead, repair its great structures, and foster national pride by perpetual allusion to the glories and sacrifices of the past.
All Members of this Chamber, and particularly those of us who are veterans on both sides of the House, join with Canadians in this pledge to our fallen comrades. We shall remember them. Their memory is green in our hearts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to be able to join with my two colleagues in offering, on behalf of this Party, and in particular on behalf of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), our Veterans Affairs critic, some words on the eve of Remembrance Day.
Each year on November 11 we pause, albeit for a moment, to remember the horrors of war, to remember those who died, to remember those who returned from the battle, broken, disabled, and in some cases devastated.
Those of us who lived through the destruction remember the bombs and sirens, and the panic and the blackouts, and the gas masks and the fears-the fear of a letter that might arrive any day from the War Office. We remember the end of the conflicts. We remember the celebration of victory, and we remember the relief tnat was felt that, at last, it was over. We remember the triumphant return of men and women to their homes and families, and the tears for those who could not return.
We vowed-I remember we vowed-never again. We vowed our enthusiastic commitment to peace. We understood that we owed a great deal to those whose lifetimes would be ones of
suffering, and we owed a great deal to the widows and families of those who had lost their lives. We were prepared to make sacrifices to make sure that those who had returned, and those who had lost, would never want.
I ask-have we kept the faith? Could we have done better? Have we truly remembered as we promised we would?
We remember all those things on November 11 each year, but that is not enough. We are once again poised on the brink-another world war, perhaps? All around, the signals warn of the possibility-armed conflict in the Middle East, armed conflict in the Caribbean, armed conflict in Afghanistan-wherever you turn in the world it seems that those who have disputes settle them by armed conflict. We see terrorism and fanaticism. We watch as the super powers play politics with weapons capable of total destruction.
1 ask, has the sacrifice of all those who went through the wars been forgotten? I do not think so, but I do believe that the passage of time dims the memory.
We have to remember every day, not just on November 11. We have to rededicate ourselves to the necessity for peace in the world, to showing by our example, our gratitude to those who fought in wars that were intended to end all wars, by taking up where they left off, and by re-echoing the plea that I remember, and I am sure many here remember-for God's sake, never again.
On behalf of my friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), whose battle for veterans has been and continues to be never ending, and on behalf of all my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, I join in paying tribute and in pleading that in the years ahead we will try to pay our debt to those who served in World Wars 1 and II, in Korea, and in the other conflicts as part of our peace-keeping effort-conflicts in which we participated willingly. I pray that we will remain mindful of the need to develop throughout the world an economic order that will eliminate poverty and want for all people, and to that end, eliminate, once and for all, the need for war.

Mr. Speaker, I have chosen to chew on my own political umbilical cord one more time. A politician who is not sensitive to the need for eternal infatuation with the news media is, to be sure, a person with lonesome neurons. Nevertheless, I elbow our centralized news media about national issues with regional roots.
November 4, 1983

For the better part of a year Canadians have heard about the Crow rate. The media would have them believe the issue deals with excessive debating, hours of petitions, Members of Parliament still speaking and poking holes in the air with their fingers at 4 a.m., and a beautiful Member of Parliament with silver, curly hair being ejected from the House of Commons. Most Canadians have come to believe that the Crow rate and parliamentary tactics are synonymous.
The majority of Canadains were never educated, however, to the fact that the Crow rate is not just a western issue but a national one. Annually it impacts on $6 billion worth of relief to our balance of payments. It affects the capacity of western producers to purchase central Canadian goods.
Some will argue, with legitimate logic, that a total payment of the Crow benefit to the railways will devastate the western meat industry and other value added economies. Others will argue that variable rates will change the map of prairie Canada, diminishing its towns and villages in favour of a few widely dispersed prairie cities.
Few realize that the present Crow rate legislation does not have the support of any of the prairie Governments or of a single prairie farm organization. Let us hope that Knowlton will give a balanced, objective, educational media report on this national issue before he "Nashes" another goodnight.

CALL FOR UPGRADING OF OVERSEAS OFFICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week in the House I spoke about the situation where Canadian immigration lawyers and consultants flocked into Hong Kong to take advantage of the difficult situation there. Some put misleading ads in the papers, and charged big fees for work the Canadian Embassy could do for nothing. It got so bad that the Embassy took out counter ads. This situation gave Canada a bad reputation.
I am happy to report to the House I have had discussions with the immigration section of the Canadian Bar Association, whose members are self policing and who report bad or misleading ads, and are trying to upgrade the status of immigration lawyers generally. I think that is a very good response. In return, I would like to ask that the Government and the Minister responsible upgrade our immigration offices in Hong Kong, Islamabad, and in Delhi. The people are burning out there. Money to improve the facilities there is tied up in Treasury Board.
There is a further problem. I warn the Government that the immigration policies themselves are inequitable. The implication is that if you are a Chinese Canadian with a brother or sister in Hong Kong, you cannot get them in under family reunification, but if you have $250,000 or $300,000 you can almost buy your way in by investing in a business in Canada. That is not really fair or just.

Mr. Speaker, Andrei Sakharov, a brilliant physicist, was the key figure in Soviet development of the hydrogen bomb. For 20 years he was a pillar of the Soviet establishment. As the years went by he saw the folly of communism and called, first, for a halt to the testing of nuclear weapons in Russia, and later declared that the state monopoly "inevitably entails servitude and compulsory conformism . . . people become hypocrites, time servers, mediocre and stupidly self-deceiving." But because communism permits no one to speak against the state he was arrested, and today he is dying without medical treatment in Gorki. 1 join with the whole free world in asking that he be given medical treatment and his freedom.
The pioneers in Canada built this country on free enterprise, but the Liberal Government has been moving Canada more and more towards a socialist state. The PC Party, under our Leader (Mr. Brian Mulroney), the next Prime Minister, will return Canada to the basic principles of free enterprises which made this country great. We will encourage the entrepreneur, the farmer, and businessman to invest and hire Canadians and expand their businesses. Profit will not be a sin, and taxation will leave some of the money earned in the pockets of the earners and producers. Like Sakharov, we will recognize that economic freedom is the best pre-condition for freedom of thought, creativity and productivity, and Canada will reach the greatness envisioned by our founders. May that day come soon!

Mr. Speaker, the Yukon Government has instituted a very restrictive requirement for people applying for social assistance. This should not be tolerated by the federal Government. In order to receive social assistance, a person must have lived in the Yukon for one year and worked for three months out of the last 12. Even long-time Yukoners must prove they have made a serious effort to obtain employment. This requirement is causing considerable hardship for people who have no other source of income and require basic help in acquiring food and shelter.
The Yukon is one of Canada's most depressed areas. The mining industry is virtually closed down. Bankruptcies have increased 100 per cent, and unemployment insurance claims are up by 86 per cent. Depleted unemployment insurance benefits are forcing workers to apply for social assistance, only to be faced with these onerous requirements.
November 4, 1983

The federal Government has a direct responsibility for social services in the Territories and must not condone these unjust requirements. However, the territorial Minister has stated that federal Canada Assistance Plan representatives, as well as federal auditors, did not object to this policy. I urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to put an end to this unjust and hurtful work requirement policy.

Mr. Speaker, we have recently heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais), and even the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), make emphatic statements regarding Canada's commitment to the western alliance and to NATO. These statements are most welcome, representing as they do a major shift in attitude by the Prime Minister who, early in his mandate as Prime Minister, sought to withdraw Canada from NATO and, failing in that regard, did bring about a very large reduction in Canada's commitments to NATO and in our over-all defence effort.
In his recent speech concerning East-West relations the Prime Minister did acknowledge that most strategists recognize that strong conventional defences have the effect of raising the nuclear threshold or, in other words, making nuclear war less likely. Most strategists also recognize that strong defences make all wars less likely, and that must surely be Canada's highest priority.
If the Prime Minister and his Ministers are sincere, they will change Canada's defence policy so as to stop the deterioration in our defence capabilities as exemplified by the fact that we still have war ships with vacuum tube electronics, replacement parts for which are only manufactured behind the Iron Curtain, and as exemplified by the fact that Canadian forces in Europe were unable to participate in the full range of the annual autumn exercises this year because of budgetary constraints.
The House and the country look forward to the Government's actions backing up the recent affirmations of commitment to defence made by the Prime Minister and his Ministers.

SETTLEMENT OF CLAIMS IN NORTHERN AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, intertwined with the constitutional process in the Northwest Territories are unsettled comprehensive aboriginal rights negotiations. These involve the Dene of the West, the Innuvialuit of the Beaufort region, and the Inuit in the central and eastern Arctic. Federal Liberal Members, in a statement in May, 1983, tied the
division of the N.W.T. to three preconditions; first, the settlement of land claims; second, the agreement of the placement of a boundary between East and West; and third, the development of the party system in the politics of the area. These preconditions, particularly the requirement for the party system, constitute a direct interference in the democratic rights of the citizens in this federal colony who are marching toward their own responsible Government.
Members of the NDP support a constitutional process for the establishment of new territories without federal interference in the form of preconditions. In concert with this would be the establishment of a new and more harmonious political arrangement between aboriginal and other Canadians in the North. We also support concentration on the development of the renewable resources of the North, including the use of small scale hydro and alternate energy programs, and we support development of the non-renewable resources of the North in the national interest but with northern control. We support a universal tax credit for all northerners, which would recognize the real differences of the cost of living in the North. We also hope that immediate measures will be taken in the North regarding the status of women in the Northwest Territories, and their particular needs.

REPORTED REFUSAL BY DOCTORS TO TREAT 10-YEAR-OLD VICTIM OF RAPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago in Alberta, a ten-year old girl was viciously raped. The very fact that this could and did take place leaves us appalled, but what leaves Canadians in an utter state of abhorrence and disbelief is the fact that the girl was subsequently denied medical treatment and examination, apparently because no doctor wanted to become involved in legal proceedings likely to follow.
Society has habitually held medical practitioners in high esteem and rewarded them accordingly. In return, society has every right to expect a high standard of ethical and moral behaviour. People expect doctors to uphold the oath they have taken. It is not something to be set aside lightly when they do not want to become involved.
The Alberta College of Physicians and Surgeons ought to investigate the incident thoroughly, and other provincial organizations ought to ensure that this could not happen in their areas.
Parliament extends, I am sure, its sympathies to the helpless victim of this crime, and reflects the feelings of all Canadians in condemning the subsequent abuse to which she was subjected.

November 4, 1983

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Transport) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
that Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the spirit with which we conducted business last night has carried over to today and will allow us, if I may draw an analogy from a movie I watched last night, to begin the "last waltz" on the Crow Bill.
I should like to say how enjoyable it has been to be a part of this interesting exercise over the past several months-perhaps we could even say years. It seems that after all this time, after the millions of words intered and the hundreds of pages of Hansard, a final round of speeches and declarations might be redundant. I believe it is useful, however, to recognize what an important and significant occasion this is. The House is engaged in final debate on a piece of legislation that will have important and beneficial significance for all Canadians for a long time to come.
This morning the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) said that in the last several weeks far too much attention has been paid by the media to the parliamentary games, the high jinks, the "Tory trot" where they bounced all over the dance floor, and the "NDP frug" where they stayed in one place and kept saying no, no, no. The concentration on those particular antics missed the point. As the Hon. Member for Crowfoot said, the media should be concentrating on the substance and depth of this Bill and the impact it will have. It has given a lot of occasion for commentary and an assessment of the machinations of the Parties as we zigzagged our way through the exercise, and certain columnists have had a chance to vent their ageing spleen on various people and personnel. The fact is, however, that the House has been engaged in a very important and significant initiative. It has been developing a basis for future growth and economic activity, not just in western Canada but in the entire country.
I think it is important that we recognize that all this took place only because of the extraordinary effort and initiative of a few key individuals. I am sure the history books will record better than I can in a short speech the names of those who played an important part in this legislation. I should like to take a moment, however, to pay tribute to certain individuals who were instrumental in bringing us to the point where we are about to decide on the importance of the Crow rate.
First and foremost I am sure Hon. Members would join me in paying tribute to my predecessor in this portfolio, the Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. Pepin), the former Minister of Transport. He was the author of the basic blueprint.

Hear, hear!
November 4, 1983

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Through his perseverance, initiative and intelligence, he was able to devise a plan and work with a variety of groups to develop a proposal. Sometimes we tend to forget that the plan was based on the most extraordinarily extensive consultations ever undertaken with any piece of legislation. Hundreds of groups and thousands of individuals were brought in for in depth discussion and examination which culminated in the Gilson report. Members of major farm organizations, railroads and shippers were brought together in one place to hammer out the architecture for the reorganization of their programs. 1 think we all recognize the important contribution that the Minister of State for External Relations has made in this area.
Some very able Parliamentarians on this side of the House helped the Minister. I mention the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael) and the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) who, as his Parliamentary Secretary, sometimes escaped both the burden and the glory. Both were able to provide backup and support in the organization of the Bill.
I should also like to pay tribute to Members of the Transport Committee who spent many months at hearings in Ottawa and across the country. They listened to over 200 briefs and gave everyone who wanted it a chance to be heard. No one was turned down. Everyone who appeared had the right to give a presentation. Members from all sides of the House were party to that very important contribution. My only regret is that the chairman of the Committee, the Hon. Member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne), is not in the House today to share in this moment. Unquestionably, of all those involved in the Committee, he was the leader. We on this side of the House would like to pay homage to his contribution to this very important piece of legislation.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
1 think it is important to recognize a number of other individuals who are not Members of the House but who also contributed. A number of very fine, highly qualified and dedicated public servants worked hundreds of thousands of hours not only in putting the Bill together, but in attending committee hearings, providing material and responding to the inquiries of Members of Parliament. Those men and women are very much part of this historical moment. A number of dedicated individuals in groups and organizations across Canada spent time on the Bill-not always in total harmony or agreement, we concede.
I think of many people from my Province who spent time in Ottawa with their organization in an effort to develop the best interests of their members and to represent the interests of the farming community and the various agrarian groups in Canada.
I want to mention all these people, Mr. Speaker, because regardless of what position was taken, no one can denigrate or downgrade the significance of what they are doing. I think it is important in this final round of debate that we clear away the sometimes intense interchange between Members of Parlia-
Western Grain Transportation Act
ment and come back to the basic consideration of what we are trying to do and what will be achieved by this legislation.
First and foremost, we are addressing the most critical factor, the most undeniable and essential ingredient in the prosperity of western agriculture, and that is the ability to move the product to market. The agrarian agricultural system of western Canada is almost unique in that it has to export virtually all its product. The geography of the west requires that the product be moved long distances by rail. Without that system of rail transportation, we could not sell. If we could not sell, we could not gain the kind of economic growth of which the entire country is the beneficiary.
One thing which has been clear for years, Mr. Speaker, is that freight rates have been a key to that development of western agriculture. However, we also have to recognize that something which has becme imbedded in history for well over 80 years must be re-examined in terms of its relevance today. What was becoming increasingly clear, not just to Hon. Members on this side of the House but to a wide variety of people, is that that system of freight rates was becoming counterproductive. It was preventing the development of a modern, up-to-date transportation system which would allow us to give certainty of market to our buyers, so that when they bought a bushel of grain from the Wheat Board or any other seller, they would be assured that the grain would be delivered on time and at a good price. We know from recent history that this is not the case right now. The reason it is not the case is that the Crow rates provide insufficient revenues to allow the railways to maintain a decent level of investment in the plant, rolling stock and maintenance of those railway lines to ensure that delivery. That is a simple, fundamental fact.
We are not going to get a good system of transportation if it cannot be paid for. If the money is not there to update it, to modernize it, to upgrade it, to make sure we have the hopper cars, the proper switching materials and the trackage, there will not be an efficient railway system which is so essential to western agriculture.
What was clear over the years is that the revenue base conditioned by the Crow was shrinking. There is an interesting article in today's The Globe and Mail which I would recommend to Hon. Members. It is the beginning of a continuing series about the CPR. It points out that when the Crow rate was first brought in, transportation represented 20 per cent of the farmers' costs. Today it represents 3 per cent or 4 per cent of those costs. Those are accurate figures and there is no one in this House who can deny it.
The fact of the matter is that over the years those rates have fluctuated up and down. However, what was becoming increasingly clear was a revenue shortfall. It does not take a great deal of wit about economics to realize that unless we can provide a system of payment to the railways to ensure a continuous, stable flow of revenue, it will be impossible for the railways to go to the capital market and generate the $15 billion or $16 billion worth of capital required in order to

November 4, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
modernize the branch lines, the main track and the communication systems. There is no lender in North America or around the world who would lend the kind of capital the railways need unless they could demonstrate they have a revenue base to justify the repayment on that capital.
All the various schemes and formulae which we have heard bandied about over the last year and a half simply do not work because they defy logic and economics. A three-year freeze, a no-freeze, a one-sale-buy-out; none of these things will work. The time has come to end the capricious ad hoc financing of our railway system and to put in place a system which will ensure a continual, ever-growing expansion and modernization of the railway service in western Canada. That is what this Bill is all about, Mr. Speaker. That is why this Government has pursued this Bill against all opposition, because we believe it is the right thing to do.
More than that, we also know that the Crow rate, over a period of time, has begun to develop as well a serious distortion in the range of agricultural diversification in western Canada. It provided disparities in the kind of costs related to one product as compared with another. As a westerner, 1 believe the future of agriculture and the future of the economy in the west is dependent upon that diversification, on a broadening of our economic base. It is dependent on allowing westerners not only to grow a wider variety of products, but to process those products in western Canada, to have value added manufacturing and development in western Canada. That is the future of western Canada. That is what westerners must build their future on. We must have that diversification, that ability to broaden the base of our economy and to eliminate those distortions in our country.
That is absolute distortion of the truth.
Pay the producer, then.

speechtext: I will get to the Hon. Member from British Columbia in just a moment. Just hold on.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

The third element of the Bill is that not only does it broaden in the long term a modern railway system and begin to eliminate the distortion-even in the present legislation, if the Hon. Member knew anything about it, which he does not-but it also unquestionably is the largest, single economic growth project in the history of Canada. We are talking about an investment of $16.5 billion of direct capital, never mind the secondary or tertiary benefits. We are talking about direct capital investment. We are talking about over
300,000	jobs. We are talking about benefits spread from one end of the country to the other.
I have to admit to being amazed at times at certain Hon. Members opposite who were standing on their feet with the utmost indignation and opposing a Bill which would have brought hundreds of thousands of jobs to their region.

growth which could fuel this economy and create hundreds of thousands of jobs?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
-because their constituents know this. The reason they were receiving those letters and telegrams saying "Quit fooling around in Parliament" is because their constituents know what this Bill will mean to economic growth in this country. 1 believe, Mr. Speaker, that has been the purpose of the Bill and that is the reason this Government has considered it to be of the highest priority.
We also recognize there are issues which have to be faced. When I was asked to take over this Ministry and met with a number of farm leaders across this country, it was made clear to me that certain issues still had to be recognized. One was the question of the ability to pay the farmers. We all recognize the kind of squeeze affecting farmers under the present grain levels-
It is too late now, you have done it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: -but what we were able to do, Mr. Speaker, is introduce into this Bill, passed last night at report stage, a major insurance policy for the farmers through the safety net.
Ten per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
If the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) would go over the historical record of grain prices, he would recognize, as 1 have just said, that at the time the Crow rate originated the farmers were paying 20 per cent of cost, not 10 per cent. There is a continuing fluctuation. If they knew anything about the economics of grain, they would recognize that.
Beginning next year we are providing a 4 per cent safety net, then 5 per cent, 6 per cent, 8 per cent, 9 per cent and 10 per cent, to ensure farmers are protected against any drastic change in the cost/price ratio. We are aware of the problem and have tried to respond with the recommendations put forward by Hon. Members. We recognized their concern and the need to provide that degree of protection and assurance so that farmers recognize this Bill is not designed to provide for a major pull-out. But it does have a ceiling on costs related to the over-all price of grain. That is the safety net and that is why I am pleased we had that amendment passed last evening. I appreciate the co-operation of Members of the Opposition in allowing that amendment to be introduced and passed.
We have also recognized, Mr. Speaker, the very important divergence of opinion over method of payment. Let us clear up
Western Grain Transportation Act
that issue. We recognize that the original proposition put forward by my predecessor included a 50/50 method of payment to producers and railroads. But it was the opposition of major agricultural groups in provinces represented by Members opposite which brought about that change. It was the pools of western Canada that demanded that the railways receive full payment. It was the organizations representing the majority of grain producers that spoke with a very clear voice to say the basis of their support is payment to the railways. On that issue we felt we had to make the change.
We also recognize that the issue is not closed. It still must be brought forward for examination. There will be a parliamentary review in 1985-86. To ensure that is simply not a re-creation of what we have had in the past several months, we have also established a special commission to bring together experts to examine the various methods of payment and determine what the impact will be so that Members of Parliament will be able to make a more learned, rational judgment about the proper method of payment to be implemented. We have given further assurances to the groups concerned that not only will the report be tabled in the House, but it will also be available for debate so there will be a clear window through which the views of the different Parties can be expressed.
These examples demonstrate we have tried to respond to the concerns and be sensitive to the issues raised. We have tried to be flexible in making changes. We have accepted many amendments, such as that put forward by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) on export definitions. Over 80 amendments have been accepted, not only in committee but during report stage. We have negotiated with Members opposite in an attempt to get the best kind of Bill. We do not claim it is perfect but we are saying it is an important beginning.
I would like to conclude my remarks by saying that we now have to implement this legislation well and effectively. The major challenge now is how to bring into full, effective implementation the many important, major steps brought forward in this Bill: the establishment of the Grain Committee, development of the Review Commission, the organization of rates and the ability to provide a more efficient and effective transportation system. We have to bring together representatives of the grain companies, the railroads, the elevators, the ports and the truckers. They are the major players and they will be required to develop the dynamics of improving the system. They will do that simply by displaying what they are prepared to do.
There are in this Bill major safeguards concerning the performance of the railways, not only through examination and evaluation by the Canadian Transport Commission, but also through the sanctions and rewards the Minister of Transport can impose if the railways do not live up to the expectations and requirements we make of them. There are a number of critically essential initiatives which must be taken. This must be done in a spirit of co-operation. It certainly would be in my interests as the Minister of Transport, and in the interests of this Government, to begin working with the farm organizations, municipalities and others involved to make this

November 4, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
Bill work for the interests of western agriculture and the interests of our country. That is our intention now. We can put the debate and controversy behind us. We have to get the Bill working.
1 invite Members of the Opposition, Mr. Speaker, to join in this effort. We recognize there is opposition, but surely they recognize how important this Bill is to their constituents and the country. I hope they will be able to put their feelings aside and, when we vote on this Bill, turn their minds to helping us bring about legislation which is written not just on paper but will begin to take on life and meaning and become one of the most important and significant milestones in the future growth and development of the agricultural system of western Canada and the economic system of our country. Members of Parliament are truly engaged in a rare opportunity to do something of major importance for the country. 1 am pleased we are now at a stage where we can all join not only in the passage of the bill but its future development and implementation.

Mr. Speaker, as is his pattern, the Minister has made an awful lot about $16 billion of benefits to the economic structure of western Canada. He will have to pardon some of us if we are a little skeptical about the arithmetic. We have been hearing about $4.5 billion for double tracking, $2.5 billion as early as 1971 at the transportation conference in Calgay, and we see these figures recycled and ballooned one on top of the other and rotated through the press for political purposes.
How fair and how sound does the Minister think that figure of $16 billion is in light of the fact that the Province of British Columbia turned the coal lands over to the CPR in a deal tied to the Crow when those lands in today's market are worth something like $450 billion? This bill does not return those lands to the Province, but rather grabs them from the Province and turns them over to PetroCan. What kind of fairness and equity and sense of well-being does he think that will develop between the people of British Columbia and the federal Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am fully aware of how the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) is an entrenched skeptic, along with some other attributes that go with that. I will take the opportunity to give him the evidence he asks for. In British Columbia we are talking about direct expenditures by the railways of $5.4 billion, which will result in 87,000 person-years of work. That will mean $3.1 billion worth of labour income, which results in about $4.4 billion of gross domestic product, and about $8.5 billion in total industrial sales.
We are talking about a major project involving over 3,000 workers in the Roger's Pass tunnel. We are talking about several thousand workers in the Prince George area. We are talking about the Valemount to Prince Rupert rail line and 400 person-years of work. We are talking about expenditure of $900 million on the main line between Vancouver and Valemount.
Those are some examples of what is going to happen in his Province, Mr. Speaker. No thanks to him because he has been one of the most obdurate, unthinking and unresponsive Members of this House to that kind of investment. Those are the kinds of projects we are talking about in immediate terms, starting now.
When we come to the question of coal lands, if the Government of the Province of British Columbia had taken any interest in the issue, it might have made some representations to us. It has not done that yet.

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions for the Minister. Before I ask those questions though, in light of the importance of the matter now before the House of Commons I think Hon. Members should be given every opportunity within the constraint of time allocation that was passed by the House to debate this Bill, and therefore, pursuant to provisions of Standing Order 8(4)(cr), I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson):
That the House continue to sit through the lunch hour today for the purpose of considering third reading stage of Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset let me indicate that it is very difficult to deal with a complex piece of legislation such as the one with which we are dealing today in one allocated day. A number of motions were presented and placed on the Order Paper. Probably between 60 and 70 of them have not been dealt with. This Bill is far from perfect; it has many defects and deficiencies. We are being asked to try to cover all its aspects in this final stage. However, I say very honestly that it is a task which cannot be achieved.
I am disappointed as well in the fact that the Government refused to allow unanimous consent on this final day of debate to provide Hon. Members on all sides with another hour in which to express their views and deal with some of the issues that have not yet been dealt with, particularly, as the Minister pointed out earlier, issues which go to the very core of the Bill. Those issues could not be debated at second reading, could not be considered at committee stage or at report stage. We are really being denied an opportunity to deal with major points, such as the method of payment, the safety net and the ability of farmers to pay.
Anyone inside or outside the Chamber who believes that with the passage of this Bill the controversy surrounding the Crow will go away is fooling himself or herself. I say that
without equivocation. My belief is that the new Crow regime which will emerge from the Bill will be more contentious and far more controversial than the old Crow. Moreover, there is no doubt in my mind nor in the minds of Hon. Members of my Party that this measure will be most oppressive to western agriculture. Unless major changes are made, it will do irreparable harm to the western agricultural economy, which is still one of our basic industries, the one upon which we rely the most and upon which Canada as a nation relies to a great extent.
When the debate started back in the middle of May, our Party expressed some very grave reservations about a number of matters. I want to deal with the more important matters. Other Hon. Members will be dealing with them as well and with other issues which relate thereto. At the very outset we expressed serious reservations about the ability of farmers to pay more for the movement of grain, particularly at a time when they have had input cost increases of 300 per cent to 400 per cent over the last ten years. Also we indicated that commodity prices had fallen to a level equivalent to 1972-73, that fuel costs had doubled in 2.5 years and that the federal Government was ripping off individual farmers to the extent of $275 million annually just in taxes. We say prairie farm incomes decline by 29 per cent in 1982. We know what happened to interest rates, a 400 per cent to 500 per cent increase. Aslo we know that 10 per cent to 15 per cent of western Canadian farmers are on the verge of bankruptcy.
We pointed out that at a time when other countries were increasing their support and subsidies for grain producers, we were going in the other direction; we were reducing ours. Based upon the last ten years, the average subsidy received by United States wheat farmers amounted to $11.41 per tonne, EEC wheat farmers were subsidized to the tune of $19.96 per tonne and Canadian wheat farmers received an average subsidy or support of $6.35 per tonne, which was primarily comprised of the transportation component, the Crowsnest Pass freight rate or the statutory freight rate. Canadian barley producers were faced with a similar situation. They received a subsidy on average over the last ten years of $6.32 per tonne, whereas United States producers received $7.57 per tonne and EEC producers received $32.80 per tonne. This study was conducted by a consulting firm commissioned by the Province of Manitoba.
When we look at Canada in relation to the United States, we find that in the 1982-83 crop year while Canadian wheat producers were supported by the federal treasury through the Crow rate by 37 cents per bushel, United States wheat producers received a subsidy of something in the order of $1.12 per bushel.
We could talk about the benefits or the breaks that Argentinian and Australian farmers receive in terms of freight rate subsidies, but I point out in passing that we are reducing our support to grain farmers while other countries are increasing their support. Whenever that happens, Canadian farmers lose because Canadian producers are price-takers not price-setters. Any increase in freight rate to producers will result in reduced
November 4, 1983

income because they cannot pass the increase on to the customers.
The second area to which we took very strong exception was the ever-escalating freight rate structure and its openended-ness with which farmers would be faced. This structure was being based upon so-called railway costs, a self-perpetuating cost-plus regime for which farmers would pay very dearly. In conjunction with that, the complexity of trying to figure out the freight rate was explained during the process of committee hearings. However, to establish such a freight rate a time frame of 2.5 years is required. Farmers will not know their freight rates for the current crop year until the freight rate cycle is completed 2.5 years hence.
The Minister has come up with a safety net. The general principle of a safety net would be supported by most people in the Chamber and indeed in the agricultural community. But when we look at the safety net which the Minister brought forth, we find on the basis of the calculations and the figures provided by the Department of Transport that for the year 1983-84 the freight rates would have to rise to $8 per tonne or grain prices would have to fall to a weighted average of SI44 per tonne in order to activate the safety net. We know very well that on the basis of the figures for 1982-83, the weighted average was $192.88. That is pretty low. It is the 1972-73 level.
As we look at the period 1990-91, in order for the safety net to be triggered, prices would have to remain the same in 1990-91 as they are today. That is not much of a safety net. It is not much protection. It becomes obvious that the farmers will essentially have to be in dire straits before this will have any effect on them. That concern still remains intact.
Third, we took exception to the fact that this Bill locked in the method of payment to the railways. We said that what it really does is, in effect, provide them with a guaranteed annual income. My friends to the left in the NDP support that principle. While they condemn the railways on the one hand, they say the money should all go to the railways. We say that this will further perpetuate the distortions that this Bill was supposed to address. It will perpetuate the same inefficiencies that have been in existence heretofore. It will perpetuate the cost-plus system. This will be paid for by the farmers and taxpayers of Canada.
Quite frankly, this Bill is not going to address those problems which this Minister was supposed to address, namely the distortions. The Minister talked today about diversification and broadening the base of agriculture, encouragement to the livestock industry and the processing industry. I say they will be worse off than before; there is no question about that. That is why in the October 24 edition of Agriweek, there is an article entitled "Prairie Groups Withdraw Support for Fed's Crow Bill". I quote from the article:
In Winnipeg, October 12, the Prairie Farm Commodity Coalition, the United Grain Growers, Manitoba Farm Bureau, the Western Feed Grains Council,
Western Grain Transportation Act
Alberta and Saskatchewan Stock Growers said that there had to be major changes to the Crow Bill.
If not, they said kill the bill.
Those allies who were on the side of the Government when the former Minister started this process have now left the sinking ship. They are not in support of it either. 1 can also quote from an independent group, the Canada West Foundation, which has passed judgment on Bill C-155. It outlines the winners and losers, and I will have more to say about this. The winners are clearly the two national railways. 1 quote from page 8 of their brief:
The losers ... under the method of payment scheme laid out in Bill C-155, the long term interests of western Canada will not be served-major losers in the Crow debate are Prairie livestock interests as represented by feed grain producer and livestock associations. Bill C-155 clearly discriminates against these groups by encouraging farmers through its subsidy structure to produce grain for export markets... the biggest losers are western Canadian agribusiness. Paying the Crow benefit to the railways deals a near death-blow to the existing and future agricultural processing in western Canada.
The Minister talked about the great splash of processing and manufacturing activity that will take place. This statement comes from an independent body, the Canada West Foundation. It is an independent think thank which has passed judgment on this. One has only to look at the groups that have come out in opposition to this measure.
What is happening is that of the four or five principles which the former Minister wanted to achieve, only one principle will be achieved. Maybe we will get more capacity in the railways. The railways will certainly get paid. They will be the major beneficiaries because this is nothing more than a sweetheart deal for the railways.
This brings me to my next point. I am pleased to see the former Minister as well as the current Minister in the House. At the time this debate started, we took exception to the generosity of this package as far as the railways are concerned. As I said, it is a sweetheart deal. It constitutes a form of corporate welfare unprecedented in this country. One has only to look at the record to confirm that.
We were also less than impressed by the so-called notional schemes, the awards and sanctions that were being imposed that would guarantee performance, efficiency and investment. We tried in the committee to tighten that up. We also tried to tighten it up in report stage. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) tried in Motion No. 58 to tighten up that provision. Unfortunately, the axe of closure fell and we were not able to deal with that motion. 1 just want to confirm what this means to the railroads. I am not picking on CPR because I think the other railway will be served in much the same way. I quote from the Wood Gundy report of July 12, 1983:
The federal initiative will add an estimated $3.50 per share in earnings in the 1983-85 period.
I quote from a recent document dated September, 1983 put out by Wood Gundy commenting on the CPR:
The Crow revision will be a primary engine of this growth which should propel the railway's net earnings to almost double their previous peak (1981) by 1985.

November 4, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
This will, in effect, double the railways' earnings over their best year ever, 1981, between now and 1985. It really is a sweetheart Bill.
We were told during the committee stage that there is at least $40 to $50 million worth of fat in this package. The two competing consultants who appeared before the committee took issue with that and documented it very accurately. These were some of the concerns that we expressed when we started debate on this issue in mid-May. We still have these concerns today. They are issues that have not been rectified. Since that time, during the course of the hearings and the six months that have elapsed, the Government has really not done anything to allay these concerns and fears. It has provided some window dressing and made a few gestures, but really nothing substantive.
During second reading debate and outside the House as well, the former Minister said that he would look at ways and means of reducing the burden on the producer. He said he would entertain the possibility of adjusting the 31.1 million tonne cap. It has been adjusted somewhat because there have been additional crops which have been brought in. He was going to look at the pros and cons of that. Also, he was again going to look seriously at the method of payment. It was really on that basis that this Bill passed second reading and went to committee. When it got to committee, we found that these matters could not be dealt with. They were found to be out of order, going beyond the Royal Proclamation or beyond the expressed intent of the Bill as it passed second reading.
What happened after that? The former Minister was dumped and a new Minister was named. He appeared before the committee, and I commend him for that, within a couple of days of his appointment. He was the epitome of conciliation and accommodation. He was going to listen to the committee. He challenged the committee to bring forth proposals with respect to the method of payment, a different freight rate structure and with respect to finding ways and means and reducing the burden on producers. He even came up with some suggestions on the agriculture adjustment fund; there was no mechanism to implement that. It was not in the terms of reference.
We have been working at this. My colleague from Wetaski-win (Mr. Schellenberger) outlined his proposal for the utilization of the agriculture adjustment fund. I commend it to the Minister because, as he says, the $204 million is still in the envelope. He recognizes, and everyone who understands this Bill just a little bit knows, that the livestock hurt is still there and it is going to be worse as more grain moves more freely to export markets. That will simply exacerbate the problem. I ask the Minister to look at the proposal of my colleague the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin.
[DOT] (M20)
The Minister appeared before the committee and said outside the committee that there was one thing that was not negotiable, and that was the method of payment. All this good will that was generated, all this conciliation and these acts of
accommodation were nothing but fluff. He had not met his caucus. As well as committing himself to one review that was included in the Bill, the Minister also committed himself to set up a special commission of inquiry under the Inquiries Act, where we witnesses can be subpoenaed and evidence taken under oath, to study the method of payment.
They also found out they had some reservations about the sweetheart deal to the railroads with respect to the constant costs, so the Government set up another study to look at the appropriateness of constant costs, which is really nothing but a profit to the railroads. The railways are going to receive full cost recovery for the movement of grain. Included in that cost recovery is a component for return on investment of anywhere from 18 per cent to 20 per cent and depreciaiton. On top of that, they are going to get a 20 per cent mark-up. It is a 20 per cent cost-plus operation. Without the constant costs the railways are still going to receive more than $1 billion a year for moving grain between their payments from the farmers, the Government the railway rehabilitation and all the other programs.
They are saying now: "Pass the Bill and we will review the impact after the Bill is passed". One review which is enshrined in the Bill is to study the impact assessment, the farmers' ability to pay, the appropriateness of the freight rates imposed upon the farmers. We have been saying: "Let us study the impact on the increased freight rates on the farmer and whether there is a better way to distribute the method of payment before we burden the producers with these exorbitant freight rate increases".
The Government have the cart before the horse. They are doing everything backward. We had a golden opportunity because there was no consensus for Crow reform and there is no consensus now. The reason there is no consensus now is that, this Minister chose to do nothing different from the former Minister. He had a golden opportunity to bring forth a new approach which would have taken into consideration those concerns of western Canada. He could and should have defended the interests of western Canadian agriculture, but he turned out to be a pygmy. He was crushed by the overwhelming influence of his Quebec colleagues. It is disturbing to westerners that, while this issue has implications right across the country, it is a western issue which is being solved-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: It is a Canadian issue.

Yes, it is a Canadian issue, but the real core of it is a western issue. The implications and the spin-off extends throughout the whole of the country but it is a western issue. The formula for Crow reform has been prescribed, not by westerners but by the politicians from Quebec and Ontario with a western Minister presiding. That is a shame and a failure. There is no question in my mind that it is going to cripple-
Say that in Quebec.

Yes, I will say it in Quebec. I will say it anywhere because it is the truth. I regret that very much. I am
November 4, 1983

surprised that the Members opposite are not receptive to hearing what the views of people in other parts of Canada are.
What are the rules on that?
Well, someone will cover that before the day is over.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Where are the pools?
Are they the Government now, Mr. Minister? Are the pools the Government now? Give away the polling and go to the pools.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Vegreville has the floor.

The Minister asks where are the pools. I do not see the pools joyously clapping their hands and supporting this Bill. They are not supporting this Bill at all. It only confirms that this Bill is going to cripple the livestock industry and could spell the demise of many farms and farm communities.
What did they tell you in western Canada?

The Hon. Member opposite who is not sitting in his seat is asking, "What to they tell you in western Canada?" I will tell him what they told us in western Canada. I am quoting from a brief that was presented by the Research Action and Education Centre, Regina, Saskatchewan. They say that on the basis of their calculations this Bill will have the effect of removing some 30,000 to 35,000 farms from rural Saskatchewan during the next decade.
Right on.

These people are worried about jobs. What about the poor farmers that are going to be driven out of business as a result of this legislation? This is not a farmers' brief. It is a brief that was put together by university academics who have an agricultural base and understand the social and economic fabric of Saskatchewan and western Canada.
I say that the Minister has been a failure. He has been overwhelmed and crushed by the influences within the Liberal caucus that have a lot more influence than he. I regret that very much because I know the Minister firmly believes that his method of payment solution is not satisfactory. I know that and I commend him for trying, but that is the way the Liberal Party operates.
Throughout the debate we have opposed those sections of the legislation which we believed to be wrong and we have proposed alternatives. We advanced a proposition that would lighten the burden of producers and give them a chance to adjust. This decision was taken after a great deal of care and deliberation. We went out and heard what the producers, communities and groups in western Canada had to say. They convinced us that the time was not ready for the dismantlement of the Crow and that this was not the time to impose an
Western Grain Transportation Act
additional burden upon the backs of producers. Therefore, we have advanced the proposition for retaining the Crowsnest Pass freight rates until the end of the 1985-86 crop year. It would not cost the treasury any money. It would just mean that during that period the railways would not get their contribution to constant costs. That is their 20 per cent profit. We are talking about something under $200 million because it is now a two and one-half year freeze since the new rates will come into effect on January 1. Mr. Speaker, that would have given the Government some time to do its impact assessment and review analysis to see what the effect would be on the individual family farm, the farm communities and the western agricultural community as a whole. They could then look at the various scenarios with respect to the method of payment and determine what effect this method or that method of payment would have upon future processing and the livestock industry.
Speaking of future processing, the canola processors are worse off now than they were before the Bill was passed and their product is being included as a statutory grain. It is ridiculous for the Minister to stand in his place and say that all these new things are going to occur.
We made a very serious proposal. It was practical and was based on common sense. It would have given the producers some time to prepared for any potential increase and we think this was the right way to go about it. It would have been fair and equitable.
We advanced proposals with respect to the method of payment. In an attempt to break the deadlock we proposed freedom of choice, not a formula delivered from on high. We challenged the western agricultural groups to examine the freedom of choice method of payment. The Alberta Government and a number of Alberta farm groups came up with the double 80 proposal. The Manitoba Farm Bureau came up with a very good proposal which would have offered freedom of choice and allowed further diversification in spreading the Crow benefit among a larger group of producers. 1 am sure there are more proposals as well. The Minister looked at them but then he said: "It is not negotiable". Mr. Speaker, what is the point of pursuing it any further? The Minister chose, instead, and elaborate review process.
Even at this late date we are merely asking that the Minister include a permissive provision in the Bill which would allow another method of payment after the review process is completed. If the inquiry comes forward with a recommendation for another method of payment, there is nothing in the Bill to allow the change to be made. We are asking that the provision be inserted so that by Order in Council, subject to parliamentary approval, a modified method of payment may be incorporated after a review. We contend that this is a reasonable and realistic proposal.
We offered amendments to include the B.C. Railway. I am pleased that the Government saw fit to allow that and, with some degree of reluctance, the Minister included the B.C.

November 4, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act Railway as an eligible railway to receive subsidies under the program.
We proposed ways and means of cutting back on the generosity of the railroads by eliminating the constant cost until we could determine with some degree of accuracy what level was appropriate. The Government suggested that the railways need the money now. They are certainly going to be a lot better off than they were previously, Mr. Speaker. They are going to get full cost recovery including return on investment and provision for depreciation. We said that was fine but that 20 per cent profit was a bit much so we backed it off. 1 wonder how many farmers operate at a profit of 20 per cent over cost. No business in the world has that kind of sweetheart deal.
We made changes to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee and tried to strengthen the role of the Grain Transportation Agency Administrator. In committee we contributed to a better bill but we cannot support the burden the Government is proposing to impose on producers and the fact that the method of payment is totally wrong. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that we maintained a responsible position. We worked hard in an attempt to seek out and prescribe a solution that would be fair and in the best interests of all.

The Minister is carrying on a conversation now. He knows that the agricultural community is divided in western Canada.

speechtext: So are you in your Party.

At least we are prepared to listen to various points of view and to work toward a solution. The Party opposite says it has the answer and come hell or high water, that is the proposal; it will be rammed down our throats.

speakerposition: Minister of State (External Relations)
speechtext: Some day you must make a decision.

All this leads to further disharmony and will strain regional tensions in the country. 1 regret having to say that, Mr. Speaker.
The concerns that existed last May exist today. In terms of the additional burden being placed on producers we say, let us see the review before we accept it. That is a logical, common sense, realistic proposal.
1 find it strange that some people are surprised that we advanced the proposal for the two and a half year freeze. Anyone who followed the debate closely might have drawn that conclusion. Anyone who followed the committee proceedings would not have been surprised. I should like to read into the record what 1 said in debate on May 12, because 1 think it will put the whole thing into perspective. As reported at page 25382 of Hansard 1 said:
This Bill will have a very dramatic impact on the economy and social lifestyle of western Canada. It is very, very difficult to gauge the degree of that impact. That is why this House and Canadians in general will have to move very slowly and deliberately on this legislation.
To begin dismantling the historic and statutory rates enjoyed by producers in western Canada is in some respects to approach the land of the unknown. The social and economic base of western Canada has largely been founded upon the production, distribution, marketing and transportation of grain. Certain patterns evolved as a result of that. The Crowsnest Pass statutory freight rate was a major component of the development of those patterns. In essence, the Crowsnest Pass statutory freight rate served as a constitutional pillar of the western agricultural industry.
I went on to talk about the difficult times that farmers were facing. As reported at page 25384 I said:
1 think a strong case can be made, therefore, for no increase until such time as the price of the farmer's commodity increases or at least reaches a level which will bear some semblance to the price of input costs and, indeed, bear some relationship to the international marketplace.
I repeated that at page 25385. The Minister of Transport was not in the House during that debate so I bring it to his attention now. I said:
This is certainly not the time to be imposing an additional burden upon the backs of the farmers of western Canada.
I repeated that and I do not know how many times I can say it. 1 then went on to outline my reasons. We expected change and accommodation when the new Minister took over but we did not get it. Today we are being asked to pass a Bill which the prairie community does not support and the Government is not prepared to listen to us.
I should like to close by saying a few things about the Bill to my urban friends. Those who live in urban areas in the country are probably sick and tired of hearing about the Crow, particularly those who live in urban areas outside the prairie basin. 1 am sure that they have some difficulty appreciating what the Crow is all about. They are not alone; we have had some difficulty as well. It is a complex issue, more complex than simply a matter of one half a cent per tonne per mile. I should like to remind them of what the grain industry means to Canada. It means in excess of $6 billion in exports. That is pretty important in terms of foreign exchange and economic spin-off. In direct employment, over 150,000 families are directly involved in the production of grain-families, not persons, Mr. Speaker. Employment in transportation and the railway system means at least another 25,000 to 30,000 people directly involved in the industry.
Rural communities, municipalities and cities exist as a result of this important industry. What does this mean in terms of spin-off? In 1981, farmers spent some $2 billion on farm machinery and parts. Most of that was spent in central Canada, in cities where people work in factories producing these important products. And farmers are very good spenders. In 1981, farmers spent $760 million on fuel and well over $200 million went directly into the federal coffers in the form of taxes. In 1981 some $642 million was spent on fertilizer and, again, a good portion of that in the form of taxes went directly into Government coffers. In terms of the multiplier effect, every dollar's worth of grain which is exported generates $4 worth of economic activity. Therefore, we are looking at something like $24 billion.

All of this translates into jobs. Of the tonnage which moves along the St. Lawrence Seaway, 52 per cent is grain. Two-thirds of that grain is Canadian grain. The Port of Vancouver owes its existence to the western farmer. Over 20 per cent of the tonnage which goes through the Port of Vancouver is grain. That translates into jobs. So when we are talking about jobs, let us not undermine that industry which produces jobs, which has jobs in place, because if the farmers are driven out of business those jobs are going to be destroyed. That is one of the points which this Government has failed to recognize.
This session opened with a Speech from the Throne delivered on April 14, 1980. At the conclusion, the Throne Speech has this to say:
Like all of your colleagues in the House of Commons, you who represent the people of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia have a responsibility to represent your constituents to the nation. You also have an extra responsibility in the present circumstances to represent the nation to your constituents. It is a task no one else can fulfil. My government is prepared to co-operate fully in helping you to achieve this.
We have a Bill before us, Mr. Speaker, which is being rammed through under double and triple closure by a Government which has no rural representation in western Canada, by a Government which has not achieved a consensus about which the Minister of Transport and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke, by a Government which does not have a mandate to tamper with the Crow because it did not mention the Crow during the last election campaign. We have a Government which is moving to invoke this Bill, which is not supported by western Canadian Members of Parliament, nor the western farmers, nor the western farm organizations, nor the western governments.
1 can only draw this conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that this Government, this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and this Minister of Transport simply cannot be trusted, because if those words in the Speech from the Throne have any meaning, they would not be proceeding with this particular piece of legislation at this time. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to amend the motion with which we are dealing as follows:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-155, the Western Grain Transportation Act, be not now read a third
time but be referred back to the Standing Committee on Transport for the
purposes of reconsidering Clauses 43, 55, 58 and 62."
