Mr. Speaker, I will certainly abide by your admonition. This could give me an opportunity to make a ten-minute speech. However, I will not seize that opportunity. 1 will try to answer the question as briefly as I can. Our bottom line has been and will continue to be to get a fair deal for the producers. This Bill does not constitute a fair deal for the producer and everything we have done in the course of the last six months has been done in an attempt to strike a better deal for the producers of Canada.
When the Minister and his Government complete all their studies on the appropriateness of the freight rate regime, the ability of the producers to pay, the method of payment and the appropriateness of the 20 per cent constant cost, all of which is going to be reviewed and studied by review committees set up by this Minister, then we will be in a better position to determine whether the producers can afford this kind of freight rate regime. The bottom line is simply that if the Government had accepted the two proposals we advanced, the freeze and the enabling provision for a modified method of payment on completion of the review inquiry, this would have gone a long way toward improving the Bill and attracting more support from western Canada. Our position has always been to try and seek out a solution in the best interests of the producer, and if it is in the best interests of the producer, then it is in the best interests of agriculture as a whole.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
If the Hon. Member is sincere in his desire to have a package worked out in the best interests of the producer, I am sure he is thinking of all producers in western Canada. He is thinking not only of the grain producers but of the livestock producers, hog and poultry producers, the specialty crop producers and so on. We heard from those producers that the Crow rate has caused a distortion over all these years. They feel they are discriminated against to the extent of 80 per cent because the grain producer pays only 20 per cent of the shipment of grain while the livestock producers have to pay 100 per cent of the cost of shipping their products. I heard this from the Hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) and others. These producers are shipping the same product, grain, but in the form of hogs or beef cattle or whatever. It is still the same product, grain, being transported, but they have to pay 100 per cent of the cost.
Would the Hon. Member explain to this House how putting a three-year freeze in place is going to correct that distortion? Will it not prolong the distortion for another three years? The NDP position would prolong the distortion indefinitely, and the Tories would prolong it for another three years. Can the Hon. Member clarify that fact? He gave us his bottom line and yet again we see there is no bottom line because they are all over the map in this situation, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport has been waving around a $204 million agricultural adjustment fund which could certainly be used to alleviate any injury to producers. If he wants to take that proposition seriously, 1 commend to him the document produced by the Hon. Member
for Wetaskiwin which answers the question the Parliamentary Secretary has advanced. Quite frankly, there is a livestock injury; there was, there is and there will be under this legislation. At least the former Minister had $204 million in the kitty to resolve that. Why does this Minister not utilize that money to relieve the livestock injury to some extent? That is what we would be doing and that is why this proposition is here.
The Hon. Member suggests that things are going to be better as a result of the increased freight rates. This is what the prairie commodity groups say. The Bill removes all incentive for increased efficiency in handling, leaving in effect a cost-plus system which will encourage the railways to maximize their grain cost structure. This system will be disastrous for grain producers who will be paying an even larger share of the enormously costly, inefficient and inadequate system that no one can afford.
The Bill goes on to say that because more grain will be moving, it will create a further distortion for the livestock producer. If the Minister and his Government are as serious about incorporating a different method of payment as they say they are, then they should be very eager to incorporate an enabling provision in this legislation. That is what we are asking for. It is a two-pronged effect but let us do it after the proper analysis and study have been done. We have spent ten years studying the so-called losses of the railway campanies. I think we can stand at least a couple of years to study the impact this proposal will have on the producers, whether they can afford to pay more, and how the benefit would best be distributed.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, one is undecided whether to try and take the high road, middle road or low road in a debate such as this. Once every 20, 30 or 50 years Parliament is faced with legislation of such consequence that it is incumbent upon people all over the country, but particularly on Opposition Parties, not only to oppose and propose, but also to try to prevent. This is one of those rare occasions.
This Parliament has sat for over three years in one session in which we have passed over 100 pieces of legislation. Some of that legislation the Opposition agreed with, some we opposed and voted against. But the Government was able to have its way. However, every once in a while, on rare occasions, a government may be embarked on a course which harms our nationhood and our Confederation. This is one of those rare occasions.
Mr. Speaker, I make no apologies for, in fact I am proud of, the role my Party and my colleagues have played from day one when we said we would do everything we could under the rules of Parliament to prevent his legislation from passing. 1 do not mean this unkindly, Sir, because I generally welcome the support of the Conservative Party in trying to prevent this Bill from passing. But it is not enough just to vote against the Bill, whether it is second reading, report stage amendments or third reading. That is easy. When we have that rare occasion when
November 4, 1983

we must try to prevent this kind of harm to our nation and our Confederation and to an important region of Canada, it seems to me, while we welcome the conversion of my colleagues from the Conservative Party on their version of the Road to Damascus, that they could have stopped this Bill back in June. They had the numbers and the rules, and they could have stopped this Bill any time after it was first introduced. They could have but they did not. They opposed the Bill, Mr. Speaker. They are in favour of stopping and killing the Crow rate but they cannot have it both ways. They do not want to abolish the statutory grain rates now. They want to do it a year and a half or two years or two and a half years from now. They cannot be half pregnant, Mr. Speaker. There is no such thing. They are either in favour of keeping the statutory grain rate for the grain producers or they are not.
Working both sides of the street is not worthy of that very historic Party. It is not worthy of Conservative and Liberal Governments that, from 1881 on, saw to it that regions of the nation were not discriminated against because of geography or because of where the goods are produced.
In all regions of Canada, Mr. Speaker, there are programs implemented by the national Government, the costs of which are shared by all the people of Canada. When we go back to the original regional programs, that concept was called the beginnings of co-operative federalism. I will never forget the first Leader of the New Democratic Party, Mr. Tommy Douglas, who campaigned in 1962 and 1963 on a platform of co-operative federalism. It was pooh-poohed by Grits and Tories at that time. Now everybody uses the phrase, and well they should because it is a non-partisan phrase and deals with the unity of the country and how we live together and deal with one another decently and fairly.
In the last few days, we have welcomed one of the few things, or perhaps the only thing, the Government has done right and that is the freeze on the St. Lawrence Seaway tolls. The St. Lawrence Seaway is essential for all of Canada, and all Canadians share in paying for its cost and losses. I would like to tell the Government that western farmers and people from western Canada supported central Canada in its bid to freeze the St. Lawrence Seaway tolls for at least one more year.
There is an attempt in the House to perpetuate a philosophy that was put forward by a Member who is neither missed nor forgotten, although I wish I could forget him, and that is the philosophy of user-pay. Members of our Party, and perhaps Members of other Parties, had access to a Cabinet document in the fall of 1981. That Cabinet document referred not only to abolishing the statutory grain rates. It also referred to the feed freight assistance Act, the At and East rates, the Maritime freight assistance Act, the Atlantic Provinces assistance Act, the deficits on the St. Lawrence Seaway and the deficits on airports. It was a document that followed up on Mr. Lang's original proposals regarding user-pay in order to get the
Western Grain Transportation Act
federal Treasury and the Government out from under all of these regional programs.
I warned my colleagues on the Government side, particularly those in the backbenches, and I warned my colleagues on the Conservative side that the statutory grain rates was just the beginning and that every other regional program was at stake. Hon. Members had best remember that warning because user-pay is indefensible when it comes to transportation since every mode of transportation is subsidized. Hundreds of commodities are subsidized. They must be subsidized in a country with our geography, our climate and our thinly and widely scattered population. There is no other alternative. We are not a nation with a large and dense population.
I do not want to say the following, but I must. It was strange how successful we were when we sought the freeze on the St. Lawrence Seaway tolls, an issue that meant so much to central Canada and to all of the ports from Thunder Bay to the Gulf of St. Lawrence. People rallied from central Canada and from western Canada to stop the increase in St. Lawrence Seaway tolls. However, Mr. Speaker, people have rallied from all across Canada to stop this legislation. It is strange that we did not get the same amount of time and attention on this issue from the Government in a year. It is only the last few weeks we have even had the time and attention of the Conservative Party.
I would like to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there are at least
200,000	signatures appearing on petitions of all kinds submitted by Members of Parliament from both Opposition Parties and submitted by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool through a Government Member. Even if 50,000 of those signatures appear on more than one petition. One hundred and fifty thousand people, most of them from western Canada, have asked that the Government not proceed with this legislation. People from coast to coast have asked the same thing. Most of those people are farmers.
The Minister spoke about rail upgrading. He proved this morning that he does not know one end of a boxcar from another. The deliberate attempt to make the grain producers and the statutory grain rate the villains of the piece is the worst kind of political chicanery that can be performed by someone who should kow better. If he knew anything about the problem, he would know better.
The Crowsnest Pass grain rates and then the statutory grain rates, have been in effect since 1897 and 1925. That, according to the Minister, was supposed to have prevented the modernizing and upgrading of the railways. Since 1897, under the staturory grain rates, there have been many improvements. During the time from 1900 to 1920, a spiral tunnel was constructed, the Connaught Tunnel was constructed and double-tracking was installed. The 1930s were kind of slow but there were a few improvements even then. The 1940s and 1950s saw the implementation of centralized traffic control from coast to coast and dieselization from coast to coast. Double tracks were installed right up until 1957 or 1958. Do you know what happened, then, Mr. Speaker? The Liberal Government followed by a Tory Government allowed the

November 4, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act railways to lift up something like 600 miles of double track in western Canada.
So much for the Minister's nonsense and his political and economic blackmail that would have us believe that if we do not raise the grain rates, we will not have the rails upgraded. If there was not another bushel of grain shipped to Vancouver and Prince Rupert starting tomorrow, those tracks would still have to be upgraded. If we moved all of the grain to Thunder Bay and Churchill and forgot about the West coast, those tracks would still have to be upgraded.
Mr. Justice Emmett Hall has made that proposition plain in his report and on several occasions since, particularly in front of the committee. He has made it plain that for the purposes of moving coal from British Columbia, the track is now almost completely upgraded from the Alberta border to Prince Rupert. That upgrading had nothing to do with grain and nothing to do with the freight rate on grain.
The statutory grain rate is a part of the charter for western Canada. We in western Canada are no different from people from anywhere else in the country. We are honest people and we deal honestly. We have always tried to operate in such a manner that a deal is a deal.
1 want to say to my friend, the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), whom I thank for repeating much of what I said in my speech at second reading, that we must cease just handing the money over to the railroads. The taxpayers, like any other investor, are entitled to have an opportunity for a return on their investment. Surely that is nothing more than good, sound business management and good free enterprise economics.
We submitted our alternative plan to the public. We mailed it to the former Minister of Transport, we mailed it to the Conservative Party and we mailed it to all the farm organizations. But I must say that we have not had the courtesy of a reply or a point by point answer from either the Government or the Official Opposition. It is the "KISS" principle which we meant mainly for the Government but which perhaps might help the Opposition. That principle is, "Keep it simple, stupid". With respect to the Dominion coal lands, all of my colleagues welcomed the fact that a Conservative Member from Alberta or British Columbia got up and supported our number one point. Our point is that the B.C. Coal lands should be returned to the Province of British Columbia. We announced our alternative program two days after the Minister's press conference in Winnipeg on February 1.
The present Minister says that British Columbia has not asked for the land back. I cannot help it if that Conservative, Liberal, Social Credit Government in British Columbia is so stupid. That is not my problem and it is not the Minister's problem. What is just and within the Constitution is the principle that the natural resources belong to the Provinces. I am not talking about offshore resources. These are inland resources in the southeastern part of British Columbia. That Province gave up many thousands of acres of that land, for
what? They did it for the Kettle Valley Railway line. But where is that line? It has been abandoned. I say that a deal is a deal and since the railroads got out of their part of the deal, surely the people of British Columbia are entitled to have their part of the deal returned. Nothing could be more simple or more just.
Our second position is the retention of the statutory grain rates for the shipping of grain from western Canada. My colleague for Vegreville spoke about the competition which exists. 1 do not need to go into that any further because he is exactly right. Our competitors in the United States, Argentina, Australia and the European Economic Community provide subsidies of anywhere from $10 to $25 a tonne. The Government is seeking to reduce the present costs of the statutory rate from $5 to $6 a tonne, to zero by 1990, even if we accepted the railways' figures. It is asking grain producers, which it has done time and time again since the turn of the century, to compete with the treasuries of the rest of the world.
What happened to co-operative federalism? According to the statutory rates, whatever the deficit or out of pocket costs, the nation as a whole shares that cost because that grain export and grain production benefits the whole nation from Halifax to Prince Rupert.
We have already lost 3,000 miles of branch lines in western Canada. Through this legislation, with its variable rates, the Government is quitting on its commitment for branch line rehabilitation and is, in fact, even transferring funds from the branch line rehabilitation account to the subsidizing of trucks, which means that many fewer miles of branch lines will be upgraded, with the loss of another 1,500 miles of branch lines.
I hope that by Monday afternoon on November 14, the Government will agree that it needs to continue to look not only at the statutory grain rates but at all the regional transportation programs. I hope it will study how they fit together in a national objective, no matter what political Party is in power. This has never been dealt with.
I want to continue my remarks, but before you cut me off, Mr. Speaker, I would like to move the following subamendment:

I want to say to my friends in the Conservative Party that this issue does not only concern wheat. I want to say to my colleagues on the Government side that it is not just wheat. The ramifications of this legislation will provide a hurt. I have yet to have anyone show me that the so-called livestock hurt is attribuable to the statutory grain rate. It is a myth for anyone to believe that abolishing the statutory rate will somehow enable western livestock producers to invade the U.S. market, whether California, the central States or eastern States and that the U.S. administration will hold still for that. If they

Mr. Speaker, this Bill has, of course, gone through several stages. First of all, in February 1982, Professor Gilson was contracted to make a full study of transportation rates for Western grain. Subsequently, the Gilson Report was submitted to the Minister of Transport, followed by publication of a statement of policy, and then the Bill was tabled in the House.
Last summer, I was fortunate enough to sit on the Transport Committee that travelled across Canada to hear witnesses and intervenors on the subject of the Bill concerning what is referred to as the Crow. Mr. Speaker, out West, I carefully followed the proceedings of the Committee and realized there was no consensus among farmers and the various agricultural organizations. As I have said several times, we deplored this. Earlier, the Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) said that the people of Quebec had forced the Government to change its position on the Bill.
1 can inform the Member for Vegreville that in Quebec we have only one association, namely, the Union des producteurs agricoles. All other organizations related to agriculture or the agro-food business supported that association, and they were merely asking to have payments made to the railways instead of to farmers, for reasons they explained in great detail.
The objective of the people who were opposed to the Bill at the time was, of course, to ensure that the policy the Government would adopt on revision of railway transportation rates for grain would not alter the competitive balance within the livestock industry in Canada. This objective was in line with the traditional claims of Quebec intervenors with respect to Canada's grain policy, which boils down to one word: equity. As far as we are concerned, the word equity in this context means different things to different people. First, as far as ranchers are concerned, equity requires that there be nothing to prevent the same basic price from applying to feed grain throughout the domestic market, in other words that there be in Canada just one domestic market. Second, equity also requires that ranchers enjoy some sort of balance in transportation costs for meat and grain. And thirdly, as far as grain producers are concerned, equity requires that they get equal treatment from the governments wherever they may be in Canada, and also that a new price allowing for adequate returns be established. At that time, and the brief was clear on that, they were asking for federal transport subsidies to be paid to railroad companies rather than to producers.
This was very important for that farm group. And at that point in time, Mr. Pierre Bornais had this to say in an editorial in the newspaper Le Courrier, and 1 quote:

Mr. Speaker, the major part of these expenditures depend on passage of the bill and on the Crow rate being changed. The railways have already undertaken their projects in anticipation of the bill being passed. They were encouraged by the decision of the Government early in 1983 to allow a depreciation allowance for railway investments. The Government has also offered the railways interim payments of approximately $300 million for the 1982-83 crop year to compensate for the losses incurred because of moving grain at the statutory price. With these payments, the railways will be able to increase their capital expenditures, namely by 40 per cent for CNR and 75 per cent for CPR. When passed the Bill C-155 will enable the railways to spend several billion dollars, and of course, to provide jobs and contribute to economic recovery in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, what will be the benefits for the provinces? In Western Canada, for instance? It has been recognized that the four Western provinces will be the major beneficiaries of the Crow rate reform. First, of course, the grain producers will benefit from a more effective and reliable railway network and rail transport system.
Everyone is aware, Mr. Speaker, that when travelling to Western Canada to hear the submissions made by residents of those provinces, all of them without exception told us that the present rail system was inefficient. I believe that this Bill will at least attempt to improve its efficiency. However, first of all, this will not prevent a reoccurrence of the congestion which occurred in 1977 and 1979 but will eliminate the need to rationalize the number of cars allotted to move each type of raw material, and second, it is in Western Canada that railway lines will be most improved. This will create jobs and provide new opportunities for local suppliers and industries. In addition, in order to assist these businesses, the Government has decided to provide $75 million worth of economic and industrial benefits as an incentive to industrial and economic development in Western Canada.
The province of British Columbia will benefit most from economic spin-offs. It is estimated that it will get 13 to more than a third of the $16 billion the railways will spend throughout the country. In Alberta, Mr. Speaker, the upgrading of the line will cost about $145 million. The CNR will spend 34 million dollars on concrete track ties manufactured in Alberta, and expand their freight stations in Japser, Edson, Edmonton and Wainwright.

speechtext: It cannot be done that way. We have already indicated that it is simply because 1 have been approached in the chair with a request for some facilitation of the program that I have mentioned it, but it is not up to the Chair to make those decisions. I cannot do that. If the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) would like to put a motion, he can do so.
Mr. Speaker, Speakers have been known not only to not see an Hon. Member but to not see the clock. That is all I was suggesting.

Mr. Speaker, I am amazed that it is so difficult to rise and give a speech on third reading of a Bill of this magnitude and importance to the country. It is a Bill that is extremely important to the prairie basin and very important to my Province of British Columbia.
The Hon. Member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ostiguy) said that all that the people in Quebec want out of this Bill is justice and equity, and he used those very marvellous words. That is all we in the West want as well, Sir. Let me assure the Hon. Member of that. I would also like to point out that I am reminded of Aleksander Solzhenitsyn's words in 1975 warning the western society of the legalistic society that is coming upon us and will be threatening our freedoms. We are certainly in the middle of that here today because, in the final hours of this debate, legalistic procedure has cut out one and a half to two speakers. During the last week we have lost a

November 4, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act day that never existed and now we have lost the opportunity for two Members from the West to speak.
I would like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that first comes the plough and then civilization. We are dealing right now with the plough of the West and the civilization of the West. The Crow rate of half a cent a ton mile made a lot of money for the railways in the beginning. It was not until the end of the 1950s and into the 1960s that inflation in the western world caught up with that statutory rate. For all those years, the Crow was a good thing for the railways and it gave the farmers of western Canada a statutory rate. They knew what that aspect of their cost would be. On the Prairies, grain prices today are the same as they were almost ten years ago. It is machinery, ingenuity, creativity and thrift that has allowed productivity in the prairie Provinces to adjust to the rising costs of energy and machinery. Now we shall see the rising costs of transportation with the removal of the protection of those costs.
As far as we are concerned, Mr. Speaker, the railways must have compensatory rates for their cost. We question if they need a 20 per cent profit on costs because who in this land can really understand the costing methods of the railways? The method of payment has been a very serious issue in the debate on this Bill. The entire payment will now go to the railway, reversing the stand taken by the previous Minister of Transport who more or less followed the Gilson line.
Throughout the debate, we have seen that the method of payment will be the heart and guts of where we will go in the future. If this Bill stands, Sir, and the subsidy goes to the railways, we have locked the West into an archaic transportation system. We have removed from the West and its farmers and industrialists the right to innovate, to put in better systems and to use other means of transportation. We have also eliminated the right of industrialists and farmers on the Prairies to have the freedom to choose what they will do with the wealth and the energy that comes from the prairie soil. That is the tragedy. Sir, and that is why some of us get so very, very emotional and upset about this legislation.
When the Minister opened the debate on third reading today, this one short day of debate on third reading of a Bill of this magnitude, he made some very disparaging remarks about the Province of British Columbia and said that if the Province had represented itself in Ottawa or had offered an opinion or statement on the coal lands, then perhaps the Government would have done something about it. I would simply like to tell Hon. Members how misleading the Minister's statement was, Mr. Speaker.
On May 20, 1983, ten days after the first reading of Bill C-155, the British Columbia Minister of Energy, Mines and Petroleum Resources sent the following message to the federal Minister of Transport:
Your proposals to amend the grain rates established by the Crow's Nest Pass Act have received support from this Province. We continue to hope for an early resolution of this issue, although we have concerns with recent changes you have made to the subsidy arrangements. We believe it desirable to pay the subsidy to the farmers and not to the railways directly. We are troubled, moreover, by the language employed in Section 62 of Bill C-155. The Province of British
Columbia has always maintained an ownership claim on the subject of coal lands. Moreover, it has regulatory requirements and land use priorities which must be met by all explorers and developers of coal. Accordingly, we trust that the federal government would never attempt to dispose of these coal lands unilaterally.
I believe it is possible for our governments to take a co-operative approach-
A co-operative approach is something about which this Government knows nothing.
-to resolving these outstanding issues in order to facilitate the orderly development of the coal resources for the benefit of British Columbia, and all of Canada.
That was the position taken by the British Columbia Government on May 20, 1983, ten days after first reading of Bill C-155. There was a limited response on June 22, 1983, to the British Columbia initiative. The government of British Columbia laid it on the line back then, Sir, and that is its position today.
When dealing with the method of payment, we keep getting it thrown back in our face that no one supports us on that issue. 1 would like to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the Government of Manitoba supports payment to the railways, but that Government is a socialist Government. What we are dealing with in this Bill is corporatism both in a state and a corporate sense. The Government will destroy the small farmer, the person with a bank debt or a mortgage on a farm. The whole damned prairie basin, Sir, will go to the big guys, the people without debt, the people with capital and the people of the second and third generations. That is what this formula of payment will do.
The Govermment of Saskatchewan is opposed to this method of payment and advocates payment to the producers. The Government of Alberta is opposed to the method of payment and believes that producers should be given the choice of how payment is to be made. It proposes the doubleeighty option. The government of British Columbia is opposed to the method of payment in this Bill and favours producer payments for reasons of efficiency. Producer groups and the pools in Manitoba support payment to the railways. The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool prefers the same method of payment as does the Manitoba Pool.
Why do the bureaucrats in the infrastructures that are locked into the railway system support payment to the railways? They are managers and elected directors and bureaucrats who manage a physical plant that is tied into the railway collection, distribution and delivery system. Of course they oppose payment to the producers because full payment or even partial payment to the producers allows some decision-making to be based at large among the population and interferes with the established infrastructure. It also interferes with the opportunity to install modern plants and find new ways of doing things with more efficiency for the delivery, production and handling costs of grain.
We find opposition all the way down the line. The United Grain Growers is opposed to the method of payment and proposes an alternate scheme similar to the freedom of choice option. Unifarm is opposed to railway payments and supports
November 4, 1983

the double-eighty proposal. Cargill is opposed to railway payments and supports the double-eighty proposal.
It is easy, Mr. Speaker, for a Member from Quebec to stand up and say that there is no consensus on the Prairies. The overwhelming consensus on the Prairies is that if we do not move to partial or full payment to the producer, we are locking in the future of western Canada.
Perhaps I can explain further, Sir, by telling you about my personal experience in a business in which 1 was once intimately involved. 1 am in the business of production of goods. I have also made my living as an efficiency expert, a critical path expert, a work study expert and a designer of better systems for handling cattle and the production of produce in the field of agriculture. That was my background. I was privy to a study that was given to me with the purpose of putting in a big packing plant and feeding operation in Lethbridge. We selected Lethbridge for many reasons. We were going to have massive feeding systems which were very efficient so that we could get a uniformity of finish on the cattle coming in.
We fed the cattle before they went to slaughter. The entrails were removed according to health of animals regulations. Hides were taken according to those regulations. The cattle were hung for curing in order to get the optimum quality out of this production. All of the tallow and bone were stripped according to health of animals protection and supervision. The meat was cut and certain cuts were ordered by hotel systems, restaurant systems and large supermarkets. This was all handled so that the maximum dollar value with no waste came out of that animal. It was one of the finest designs and one of the best economic structures in meat handling, from hoof all the way through to store shelf and the plate on the restaurant table, that we had seen. I was part and parcel of this.
That operation was uneconomical in the Canadian Prairies because the subsidy moving the grain out to the large areas of consumption made it impossible to move the finished product. That is why 1 stand here to say that what the Government is doing is wrong. It is smothering and suffocating the West with its stubborness and adherence to this concept of payment to the railroad. It is all right to say that we will set up a study of the matter which will examine it and that perhaps two and one-half years from now, when the committee reports back, we will change the Bill. One of the amendments my colleague for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) was asking for was an amendment to the Bill so that recommendations from that study could be put into the Bill. Therefore, if we have to follow a modified Gilson formula or whatever the committee decided flowing from its studies, something could be done that would give some staying power to the future and the infrastructure of the region I come from.
You cannot question my love of the country but do not blame me for being raised and educated in the West. I understand and love this country. I understand and love the freedoms that it has given me and allowed me to pass on. But I
Western Grain Transportation Act have a western sense about me, the same as the people from Quebec have a Quebecois sense about them. I am saying that if you want to keep this country going, regions that have political power in this House must not impose that power arbitrarily on the rest of us. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this week in Edmonton a new federal Party was formed. It is called "The Confederation of Regions' Party". That Party will address this regionalization of Canada if we in the House cannot.
Bill C-155 and the arrogance and manner with which it is being imposed upon us has produced an anger that will last and stay unless we fix it.
I do not have enough time to say the rest of what is in my heart. I really want that time but I am going to sit down after speaking for 15 minutes because I know that I have some colleagues who really want to express in the final minutes of this debate how they feel and how their regions feel about this Bill. But I tell those Members on the Government side that what they are ramming down our throats in the West with this Bill, on top of the National Energy Program, will not be forgotten. It will not heal the wounds of this country; it will aggravate them. With that, I will sit down and allow somebody else to speak in the few remaining minutes.

I want to remind the House that the subamendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) was found to be in order. Accordingly, I will put it to the House. Moved by Mr. Benjamin, seconded by Mr. Althouse:
That the amendment be amended by adding Clauses 33, 41,47, 54 and 59.
As I already indicated to the House, the amendment is in order. The Chair will now call for questions, comments and answers for ten minutes related to the speech of the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). At that time I will look to my right for the next speaker. Debate will close at 4.45 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, the problem with the Crow rate has been before this House for years. I came here in 1979 and served on the Transport Committee, it was evident that the Government of the day, with the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) as Minister of Transport, had to look to the Crow rate. It had to be one of the priorities for resolution in the very near future. It was a problem that would not go away and had to be faced, not deferred.
The previous Minister of Transport, now the Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. Pepin), established the Gilson task force. That task force came as close as possible to reaching a consensus. During the interim, unfortunately, different associations which had been part of that consensus allowed it to disintegrate because they were trying to bargain for more. The Gilson report was then amended and submitted.
In the P.C. dominated Provinces, the Gilson report as amended was slow to be endorsed. Subsequently, when we made our tours across the country, people said that we should

November 4, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
have adopted the Gilson report, but 1 must confess that we found no unity in the West on the resolution of the Crow. Many witnesses in Alberta told us that they would rather proceed with the present Bill with the expectation of amending it at a later date or making changes from the experience garnered rather than do nothing. When we went to British Columbia, the witnesses there told us emphatically to proceed and get on with the Bill because the country needs it. In Manitoba, many people said that they did not want any change at all but, on the other hand, they wanted increased benefits, improved capacity and to make sure the railway employees have work. But they did not want the Government to add any cost to the producers.
When we returned from the hearings which the Transport Committee held in the West we resumed our meetings in the Railway Committee room.
The Official Opposition launched its trial balloon saying that there should be freedom of choice. It was a nice catch phrase which can also apply when talking about abortion. The Conservatives advocated freedom of choice for the producers. They let that lapse and took the position that it is better to do nothing. Rather than make a decision they wanted to put a freeze on the rates and wait to see what happens. They suggested that we should gain three years of experience and proceed in the meantime with putting in the required infrastructure to improve the capacity of rail and product transportation to export.
There is no doubt in my mind that costs for producers have gone up. We recognize that grain producers are in a class by themselves. They do not have the option of passing on their production costs to the customer because of our system for marketing our cereal grains to export. Producers pay more for land, shelter, farm buildings, their equipment and supplies. That is not an exception to the rule. Show me a business that has not had increased costs. Everything has gone up, everything costs more. Show me a consumer whose costs of living have not gone up. Every business would like to have the guarantees given to grain producers. They have been guaranteed an adequate transportation and a safety net which will keep the percentage of the sale of their goods limited, so that they do not pay more than a fixed percentage to transport their grain. No one in the country, if invited, would want to pay more taxes. No one wanted to pay more for postage. No one wants to pay more for services.
What it boils down to is the fact that producers do not want to pay more for transportation. As was mentioned earlier today, their transportation costs represent 3 per cent to 4 per cent of the sale price of cereal grain. They do not want to pay more than that.
What does the federal Government propose to do to assist western transportation initiatives? Having established the datum of the Crow benefit at $650 million, Canadian taxpayers will continue to contribute in perpetuity at least $650 million toward the transportation of cereal grain. Last year
producers paid $135 million for something that cost $785 million to handle. As increases are applied to the cost of transportation, producers will only have to pay twice as much in four crop years; they will be expected to pay twice as much for transportation in four crop years as they do today. There is a myth propagated that it will be five times Crow by 1991. There will be a review after four crop years. In anticipation of the review, we will look at the experience. The Opposition says that we should do nothing for three years and then look at what is possible. In that event we would defer ad nauseum what we will do for grain producers.
The Canadian Government is looking to spending $3.5 billion in the next 3.5 years, that is $1 billion per year. First there is the $650 million subsidy. Then there are the branch line rehabilitation fund, branch line subsidies and hopper car purchases and leases for which the Government of Canada pays. That runs close to $1 billion per year. We are doing a great deal to help grain producers.
Also the Government has taken initiatives in the area of helping to establish a superport at Prince Rupert, to improve the Port of Vancouver and to improve rail lines. These improvements will make it easier for grain producers and all suppliers of manufactured and processed goods and mineral resources across the country to receive goods, to transport them across the country and to export them. This is the catalyst which will cause the railways to spend $16 billion in the next eight years.
It has been mentioned by other speakers in the House how that $16 billion will be apportioned to the various regions of the country, how it will improve the economy and create jobs. Our intention is to create jobs, to provide employment and to enhance the economy. It is important that it be done on a broad spectrum to help everyone across the nation and to give the country the railway system and transportation it needs. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity to travel in Saskatchewan where I met people who have been in wheat and grain production for years. The tradition was passed on from grandfather to father to son, and those people have told us: Ah, there is one thing which you should not do, and that is change the Crow rate.

For those people the Crow rate seemed to be a dogma of faith. We could not touch it. When we asked why, they really did not know. It was because they were told from generation to generation that they must never spend more on transportation. They had to spend more on everything else, but it was one thing on which they should not have to spend any more. That defies logic. It is necessary to realize that when everything else is costing more, people are prepared to meet what the Canadian Government wants to do.
May I in closing-
